summary: Describes the UniDirectional Link Detection (UDLD) protocol from Cisco, which detects and disables Ethernet fiber or copper links where traffic flows in only one direction, for example because of miswired fibers. It works at Layer 2 and is documented as a possible base for future standardization. It is informational and describes a vendor protocol.

eli5.summary: Imagine a phone line where you can hear them but they cannot hear you. UDLD notices this one-way problem and turns the line off so it does not cause trouble.

questions: how to detect unidirectional ethernet link
how does udld detect unidirectional links
subtitle: Detecting and disabling Ethernet links that work in only one direction.

tldr.problem: Miswired fiber or hardware faults can create Ethernet links where traffic flows in only one direction, breaking protocols that assume bidirectional communication and creating network loops.
tldr.mechanism: UDLD is a Layer 2 protocol that periodically advertises device and port identity and echoes neighbor information back to confirm mutual bidirectional visibility before considering a link active.
tldr.outcome: Unidirectional links are detected and disabled, preventing Spanning Tree loops and other protocol failures caused by broken assumptions about two-way communication.

today: RFC 5171 documents the Cisco UDLD protocol as informational. While not an Internet standard, UDLD is widely deployed on Cisco switches and is part of network design best practices. The RFC serves as a technical reference and possible base for future standardization. A related standard, Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD), provides similar link detection at a different scope.

sections.title: The Problem: One-Way Links
sections.content:
Ethernet switches use the Spanning Tree Protocol (STP) to create loop-free network topologies and rely on the assumption that links work bidirectionally: if one switch can send to another, the other can send back. Miswired fiber strands or hardware faults sometimes violate this assumption, creating links that carry traffic in only one direction.

For example, if RX (receive) fiber is patched to the wrong neighbor and TX (transmit) fiber to another, a port may appear active (it receives light) but cannot send traffic in return. Such unidirectional links cause Spanning Tree loops and protocol failures. UDLD detects and disables these broken links before they cause damage.
sections.eli5: Network switches talk to each other using fiber cables. A mis-patched cable might let them hear but not be heard. UDLD notices this one-way problem.

sections.title: Protocol Design and Operation
sections.content:
UDLD operates at Layer 2 (the data link layer) on top of existing Layer 1 (physical layer) detection mechanisms. It uses two core mechanisms: periodic advertisement of device and port identities via hello messages (also called probes), and event-driven echo messages that repeat back the neighbors seen on a port.

Each switch maintains a neighbor database (a cache) of devices and ports seen on each interface. When a hello is received, it is cached for a defined holdtime. If a device is reset or a link goes down, UDLD sends flush messages to keep all neighbor caches consistent.

The detection process works through echo messages: when a new neighbor is discovered, UDLD begins sending N echo messages that repeat back the neighbor identities seen on that port. If the neighbor receives these echoes and responds, bidirectionality is confirmed. If no proper echoes are received, the link is considered unidirectional.
sections.eli5: UDLD sends messages saying "I hear you from port 1 on my device," and waits for the other side to say "I hear you too." If they never say it back, something is wrong.

sections.title: Normal and Aggressive Detection Modes
sections.content:
UDLD supports two operational modes:

Normal mode is conservative: it shuts down a port only if it can explicitly determine that a link is unidirectional (based on absence of proper echo information). If bidirectional communication fails entirely, normal mode leaves the port in an undetermined state rather than disabling it. This approach minimizes false positives.

Aggressive mode is more proactive: it shuts down a port if bidirectional connectivity is lost for an extended period, even without explicit proof of unidirectionality. This mode assumes that loss of communication is itself a meaningful failure symptom. Aggressive mode is recommended only on point-to-point links where complete communication loss is unacceptable and where false positives can be tolerated.
sections.eli5: Normal mode says "I only turn you off if I know you are broken." Aggressive mode says "If you stop talking I assume you are broken and turn you off."

sections.title: Packet Format and Message Types
sections.content:
UDLD packets are encapsulated in Ethernet frames using the SNAP (Subnetwork Access Protocol) format. The packet header contains version (3 bits), opcode (5 bits), flags (8 bits), and checksum (16 bits).

The opcode identifies the message type: Probe (0x01) is the periodic hello message, Echo (0x02) repeats neighbor identities, Flush (0x03) signals cache invalidation. The payload consists of Type-Length-Value (TLV) fields.

Key TLVs include Device-ID (uniquely identifies the sender), Port-ID (identifies the physical port), Echo TLV (list of neighbor device/port pairs seen), Message Interval (how often to send probes), Timeout Interval (detection timeout duration), Device Name (user-readable name), and Sequence Number (message counter for debugging). All UDLD implementations must use IP-like checksums.
sections.eli5: The message format is simple: who you are, what port you're on, who you have heard from, and how often you're going to say hello.

sections.title: Protocol Timers and Operational Behavior
sections.content:
During the detection phase when a new neighbor is discovered, UDLD sends messages at the maximum rate of one per second. After detection completes, if the link is deemed bidirectional, the message interval increases according to a time-based function M1(t): it stays at Mfast (7 seconds in current implementations) for the first 4 transmissions, then transitions to Mslow (default 15 seconds, configurable up to 90 seconds).

If the link is not bidirectional, it remains at Mfast. This conservative approach prevents false positives due to timing variations in software/firmware and CPU scheduling delays. UDLD runs in the control plane of the switch, not the forwarding hardware, so detection speed is limited by CPU responsiveness rather than link speed.

If a fault is detected, the port is held down for a predetermined time before recovery is attempted, avoiding unnecessary link flapping.
sections.eli5: After confirming a link works both ways, UDLD slows down to save CPU time. If a problem is found, the port stays down for a while before trying again.
